morphemes.formRelation: direct
TRACT reflects the tract- form seen in Latin tractum; not a standalone Latin lemma.
DUC follows the verbal base; DUCT reflects the duct- form seen in Latin ductum.
SCRIPT reflects the script- form; Allen & Greenough documents the phonetic development scriptus from an earlier scrib-tus sequence.

MIT is the root-level teaching form; MISS reflects Latin missum. Allen & Greenough §176 explicitly analyzes mitt-i-tis as root MIT with consonant doubling in the present stem, so MITT is not published as a separate morpheme.

CAP/CAPT are directly grounded in capio/captum. Latin compounds recipio and accipio, explicitly marked from capio, directly attest the -cip- present-stem and -cept- participial forms. CEIVE/CEIT remain later Romance/English transmission forms.
PRAE- is the attested Latin form from prae. English PRE- is a downstream historical reflex and is intentionally not asserted by the source-language authority layer.

morphemes.formRelation: Variant behavior follows Latin phonology.
Allen & Greenough lists de- in compounds with the adverbial values down / utterly.
Assimilation may occur in compounds, but no learner-facing variant is published here until each form is explicitly represented and tested.
FIN is the pedagogical form tied to Latin finis; downstream English-word membership must be verified separately.
PEND is tied to the Latin pendeo family; downstream English-word membership is a separate claim.
Allen & Greenough lists ante- as a verbal prefix retaining the adverbial sense BEFORE.
Allen & Greenough lists circum- with the adverbial sense AROUND.
Allen & Greenough lists super- with the senses UPON / OVER AND ABOVE.
Allen & Greenough treats dis-/di- as an inseparable particle with the senses ASUNDER / APART.
Allen & Greenough lists red-/re- as an inseparable particle with the senses BACK / AGAIN.
Allen & Greenough lists sed-/se- as an inseparable particle with the sense APART.
LSJ explicitly records αὐτός in compound use with the value self-/of or by oneself.
LSJ explicitly describes σύν in composition as with / along with / together and as marking union or connection.
Smyth explicitly identifies root γραφ and gives λογο-γράφο-ς as a compound; GRAPH is the conventional Latin-letter teaching transliteration of γραφ-.

stemDerivation.method: explicit root in Smyth; compound evidence in λογο-γράφο-ς

morphemes.formRelation: Smyth explicitly gives λογο- as the stem of λόγος and λογο-γράφο-ς as a compound; LOG/LOGO represent that attested stem family.

stemDerivation.method: explicit noun stem in Smyth and compound λογο-γράφο-ς

morphemes.formRelation: βίος is a second-declension noun; Smyth defines the second declension as O-stems, supporting βιο- as the source stem. BIO is the Latin-letter teaching transliteration of βιο-.

stemDerivation.method: second-declension O-stem rule applied to attested βίος

morphemes.formRelation: LSJ attests γεω- in γεωγραφέω 'describe the earth's surface'; GEO is therefore tied to an attested Greek compound form, not inferred from English spelling.

stemDerivation.method: attested compound form γεω- in LSJ γεωγραφέω

morphemes.formRelation: LSJ identifies ἄφωνος as formed from φωνή, directly exposing φων- in composition. PHON is the Latin-letter teaching transliteration of that attested compound stem.

stemDerivation.method: attested compound form in LSJ ἄφωνος (from φωνή)

morphemes.formRelation: Allen & Greenough §267 lists a/ab as verbal prefixes retaining the adverbial sense AWAY.
Allen & Greenough §267 lists amb- with am-/an- variants and the sense AROUND.
Allen & Greenough §267 lists por- as an inseparable particle with the sense FORWARD.
Allen & Greenough §267d explicitly treats per- as an adverbial intensive prefix meaning VERY. This record does not cover prepositional per 'through'.
LSJ gives the radical sense THROUGH and attests διά as a productive prepositional element; DIA- is its Latin-letter teaching form.
LSJ attests μετά with genitive/dative senses around WITH/AMONG and accusative AFTER. Downstream English senses such as 'meta-' = self-referential are not owned by this authority record.
LSJ explicitly describes παρά in compounds with beside/alongside, past, and beyond/amiss relations.
LSJ gives περί the core spatial sense AROUND / ROUND ABOUT; PERI- is the Latin-letter teaching form.
LSJ explicitly treats πρό in compounds with BEFORE/FORWARDS and related senses. This Greek PRO- record is distinct from Latin pro-.
LSJ explicitly states that ὑπέρ signifies OVER/ABOVE and documents compound uses including excess beyond measure.
LSJ gives ὑπό the core spatial senses UNDER / FROM UNDER; HYPO- is the Latin-letter teaching form.

Lewis & Short explicitly identifies root dic- and derives dictio from dico; compounds such as praedico preserve the dico family and show the dictum/-(d)ict- participial branch. DIC/DICT are source-language grounded.

FAC/FACT are directly grounded in facio/factum. Latin compounds such as conficio directly attest the -fic- present-stem branch and fectum; FIC is therefore source-language grounded. FECT remains a downstream English teaching mapping, while FEC is not published as a separate morpheme.

FER follows the present/infinite family of Latin fero/ferre. LAT reflects the suppletive participial form latus/latum, explicitly linked by Lewis & Short to fero. LATE remains a downstream English teaching form.
MOV follows the moveo/movi family; MOT reflects the mot- form in Latin motum.

PON follows Latin pono; PONE is directly grounded in the infinitive ponere; POSIT reflects the posit- form in Latin positum. POS/POSE/POUND are not source-language aliases and require separate disposition or transmission evidence.
PORT is directly tied to the Latin porto/portare family.
RUPT reflects the rupt- form in attested Latin ruptum; Lewis & Short explicitly gives the root rup and the break/burst/tear sense family.
SENT follows the present family of sentio; SENS reflects the sens- form visible in sensi/sensum.

Lewis & Short directly records specio with the variant spicio; Latin compounds such as inspicio preserve the spic- form and record spexi, spectum. SPEC/SPIC/SPECT are therefore source-language grounded. SPECTRO remains outside this authority record pending later derivational evidence.
STRUCT reflects the struct- form in Latin structum; Lewis & Short gives struo with the meanings place upon one another, pile up, arrange, build.
TEN follows the present family of teneo; TENT reflects the tent- form in Latin tentum. English TAIN is a later historical reflex and is not asserted here.
VEN follows the present family of venio; VENT reflects the vent- form in Latin ventum.
VOC is directly tied to the Latin voco/vocare family. English VOK spellings are not source-language forms and are excluded.
VID follows the video/vidi family; VIS reflects the vis- form in Latin visum.
FORM is directly preserved in Latin formo/formare. Lewis & Short defines formo as to shape, fashion, form.
GRAD is visible in gradior; GRESS is the attested participial/perfect-family form gressus.

Lewis & Short explicitly identifies root sta- under sto; STAT reflects statum, while STANT is directly visible in the participial/adjectival branch constans, -antis. STANCE is downstream Romance/English and is not a Latin source form.
CED is visible in cedo; CESS reflects the cess- forms cessi/cessum. English CEED is intentionally excluded from this Latin authority layer.
Lewis & Short records cludo as a frequent compound form of claudo and clausi/clausum as the closed-form family; CLUD/CLUS are therefore source-language grounded.
CURR is visible in curro; CURS reflects the curs- form in Latin cursum.
Lewis & Short explicitly marks root GEN under both gigno and genus; the oblique stem gener- is directly visible in Latin generis. GEN/GENER are therefore source-language grounded.

VIV is directly grounded in Latin vivo and the related adjective vivus. VIVI is an inflected/sequence form rather than a separately published morpheme; VIT belongs to the vita/vitalis path and is not collapsed into VIV.
VITA is the attested Latin noun vita 'life'; Latin vitalis is explicitly derived from vita. The learner truncation VIT is not published as a source-language morpheme.

Lewis & Short compound entries for proicio/projicio and deicio/dejicio directly record jeci, jectum and identify jacio as the source verb. JECT is therefore an attested Latin compound-stem form, not an English-only teaching invention.
VERT follows Latin verto/verti; VERS reflects the vers- form in Latin versum. Both are directly source-language grounded.

coreMeaningEn: that by which anything is measured
morphemes.formRelation: LSJ defines μέτρον as a measure and attests μετρο- in compounds such as μετρονόμοι and περίμετρον. METR/METRO are Latin-letter teaching labels for the attested Greek stem/compound forms. English METER/METRY are not asserted in this source-language layer.

stemDerivation.method: attested noun/compound forms in LSJ: μέτρον, μετρονόμοι, περίμετρον

morphemes.formRelation: Lewis & Short gives Latin pes, genitive pedis, 'foot'. PED is the source-language stem visible in pedis. PEDI/PEDE are not published as independent Latin morphemes.

Lewis & Short defines actio as derived from ago and as doing/performing/acting; compounds such as adigo directly preserve the ago family with egi, actum. AG/ACT are therefore source-language grounded.
LSJ defines μόνος as alone/single and directly attests μονο- in compounds such as μονογενής. MON/MONO are Latin-letter teaching labels for that verified Greek family.

stemDerivation.method: attested compound form in LSJ μονογενής and related mono- compounds

morphemes.formRelation: LSJ defines στάσις as standing/posture and directly derives στάσιμος from στάσις, exposing the stas-/stasi- stem family. STAS is kept separate from Latin STA/STAT/STANT.

stemDerivation.method: attested noun στάσις plus derivative στάσιμος in LSJ

morphemes.formRelation: Lewis & Short directly records trans as a Latin preposition and compound prefix, and states that in some phonological environments the compound spelling varies between trans- and tra-.
Lewis & Short gives Latin tres/tria 'three' and explicitly notes tri- in the etymological formation of tribus. TRI is therefore source-language grounded rather than inferred from English compounds.

REG follows Latin rego; RECT reflects rectum; Lewis & Short directly records corrigo as a compound of rego, grounding the -rig- compound form. REG/RIG/RECT therefore stay in the source-language authority layer.

LSJ defines ὕδωρ as water and directly attests the compound form ὑδρο- in ὑδροφόρος 'carrying water'. HYDRO is the Latin-letter teaching label for that attested Greek compound form. HYDR remains outside the authority layer pending a separate derivational analysis.

stemDerivation.method: attested compound form ὑδρο- in LSJ ὑδροφόρος

morphemes.formRelation: Ancient Greek ἐπί functions as a preposition and compound prefix; LexiFlow publishes only the conservative EPI- teaching form here. EPH-/EP- remain deferred until their elision/euphony rules are represented by an approved grammar source.

JAC is kept separate from JECT. Latin iaceo/jaceo is the stative 'lie/be situated' family seen in adjacent-type formations, whereas JECT belongs to iacio 'throw'. The discovery candidate conflates these related but semantically distinct Latin families.
BIS is the attested Latin numeral adverb meaning twice. English BI- is modeled downstream rather than being inserted as a Classical Latin teaching form without a direct source-language entry.
BINI is the attested Latin distributive numeral. English BIN- is treated as a later learned/Romance variant rather than as an independent Classical Latin prefix.

CAPIT is directly visible in the genitive capitis. Latin praeceps has genitive praecipitis and Lewis & Short explicitly analyzes it as prae-caput, directly grounding the compound CIPIT form. This head-family is distinct from CAP/CIP/CEPT < capio 'take'.
